old: Abhi tak char dishes hain, jaldi mein nahi hain, sahi karna zyada zaroori hai.
new: Abhi tak char dish hain, jaldi mein nahi hain, sahi karna zyada zaroori hai.
why: Urdu doesn't take the English plural '-s' on a borrowed noun once a number already marks it plural ('char dish', not 'char dishes') — the same pattern the calendar already uses correctly elsewhere ('Result season', not 'Results season'). 'Char dishes' reads like a direct English insert, not something a Lahori would actually say.

old: Abhi tak char dishes, jaldi mein nahi hain.
new: Abhi tak char dish, jaldi mein nahi hain.
why: Same fix as the caption, for consistency within the same post: 'char dish' not 'char dishes'.

old: Barf zyada, iss par koi behas nahi hoti.
new: Barf zyada, is par koi behas nahi hoti.
why: Spelling consistency: 'is' (this) is spelled with a single 's' elsewhere in this same calendar (muharram-quiet-note: 'is dauraan lehja...'). 'Iss' is the only doubled-s instance in the file — standardising avoids the same kind of drift the earlier roman-urdu-review.md caught with 'baqi' vs 'baaki'.

old: Joon mein Lahore ka ek hi usool hai, aakhir mein aam zaroor aayega.
new: June mein Lahore ka ek hi usool hai, aakhir mein aam zaroor aayega.
why: The brand book's spelling table keeps English loanwords in English, not phonetically respelled ('scan', 'table', not a Roman-Urdu version). Month names follow the same logic — a Lahori would text 'June' with a Roman Urdu sentence around it, not the phonetic 'Joon'. The slide headline in the same post already uses 'June' correctly ('Lahore in June'), so this also fixes an internal inconsistency.

old: One of the quieter benefits: fewer table-side questions about what a dish actually looks like, since guests already saw it before ordering.
new: One quieter upside to expect: fewer table-side questions about what a dish actually looks like, once guests have already seen it before ordering.
why: States an operational result ('fewer table-side questions') as an established fact. Nothing in BRIEF.md or the brand book confirms this — the pilot's analytics exist but haven't been measured yet (brand-book Section 8: 'No AOV or "orders increased" claims about MENVA itself exist yet'). This is the same kind of unverified-benefit claim, just about waiter time instead of sales. Hedging it as an expectation keeps the sentence honest without losing the point.

old: "Yeh kaisi dikhti hai" wala sawal khud hi khatam ho jaata hai.
new: "Yeh kaisi dikhti hai" wala sawal aksar khud hi khatam ho jaata hai.
why: Same claims-policy fix as above, in the Roman Urdu line: 'aksar' (often/usually) turns a flat, unverified claim into a plausible, hedged one.

old: Guests answer that one themselves before the waiter arrives.
new: Guests can often answer that one themselves before the waiter arrives.
why: Same claims-policy fix, in the slide subtext: states a specific outcome as settled fact when it hasn't been measured yet. 'Can often' keeps the line calm and plausible without an unearned guarantee.
